sentences.text: The holotype skeleton of Epidexipteryx hui measures 25 cm in length and was estimated to weigh 164 grams.
This well-preserved partial skeleton includes four long tail feathers composed of a central rachis and vanes.
Unlike modern tail feathers, the vanes of these structures were made of a single ribbon-like sheet rather than individual branched filaments.
The skull of this animal resembles those of Sapeornis, oviraptorosaurs, and therizinosauroids.
Epidexipteryx possessed teeth only in the front of its jaws, with long forward-angled teeth similar to those of Masiakasaurus.
The tail vertebrae resembled the pygostyle found in modern birds and some oviraptorosaurs.
It had a hip configuration where the pubis was shorter than the ischium, a trait similar to Scansoriopteryx.
The rest of the skeleton preserved a simpler body feather cover made of parallel scales similar to those of more primitive feathered dinosaurs.
Epidexipteryx represents the earliest known dinosaur genus with ornamental feathers in the fossil record.
Researchers have hypothesized that this creature used its long claws to dig for grubs in trees, similar to the aye-aye.
The formal description of Epidexipteryx was published in the journal Nature on October 23, 2008.
The species name Epidexipteryx hui honors paleomammologist Hu Yaoming, whose name means "Hu's display feather" in English and "Hu Yaoming's display dragon" in Chinese.
The fossil was found in the Daohugou Formation of Inner Mongolia, dating to approximately 168 to 160 million years ago.
Epidexipteryx likely lacked wing feathers but may have had a membrane wing for gliding, similar to the related dinosaur Yi.
The exact phylogenetic position of Epidexipteryx within the group Paraves remains uncertain.
A 2024 study by Cau suggests Epidexipteryx may be a junior synonym of Epidendrosaurus due to incomplete fossil evidence and variable traits.
The authors of its description recovered Epidexipteryx as a member of the family Scansoriopterygidae and as a basal member of the clade Avialae.
A separate exploratory analysis recovered Scansoriopteryx/Epidendrosaurus as a basal Avialae member unrelated to Epidexipteryx, which remained outside Eumaniraptora.
Epidexipteryx belongs to the parent group Paraves and is classified within the class Reptilia.
Epidexipteryx lived in the Middle or Upper Jurassic of Inner Mongolia, China, approximately 160 to 154 million years ago.
Epidexipteryx lived during the Callovian stage, from 165.3 to 161.5 million years ago.
Zhang et al. suggest that unless Epidexipteryx evolved from flying ancestors that later lost their wings, its advanced display tail feathers may have preceded flight or gliding.
